source.title: Computation in Superposition: Two Handcrafted Models

record.tranche_reason: The post studies how toy networks implement name-pair classification, but does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or test any listed polysemanticity version.
record.gate_note: The post reports learned computation strategies in toy networks. These findings do not measure polysemanticity as defined in the claim versions; the related mechanism findings are recorded under fits_no_version. The handcrafted examples are not results about trained networks.
record.test_reason: The post builds and trains toy networks on an eight-pair name-memorization task and describes their mechanisms: additive voting versus subtractive cancellation. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, or how often. It does not vary capacity, activation, architecture or measurement method to test any version. Its subject is computation in superposition, not neuron polysemanticity rates or causes.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that trained networks on this toy task mix additive superposition-based computation with a subtractive encoding that sidesteps superposition. They hypothesize that the additive mechanism may matter when downstream computation needs to keep track of which entity was identified.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a toy supervised name-pair memorization task and analyzes learned computation strategies, rather than measuring polysemantic neuron responses as in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The post says the two-neuron solution is reliably recovered with negative initialization; without it, additional help such as aggressive cosine annealing or minibatch noise may be needed. Perturbation noise around 10% of parameter magnitude reduces accuracy but further training can restore the perfect solution; stronger noise is increasingly difficult to recover from.

fits_no_version.finding: A trained six-neuron network on the name-pair task used a hybrid mechanism: some neurons voted additively for famous pairs, while neuron pairs voted subtractively against non-famous pairs. A trained two-neuron LeakyReLU network recovered the purely subtractive solution, reliably with negative initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks trained on toy fact-memorization tasks can mix computation in superposition with low-dimensional encodings that avoid superposition.

record.problems: The results concern a restricted toy task with eight famous athlete pairs. The post gives no uncertainty estimates or explicit control comparisons for the reported learned mechanisms.
record.rows_left_out: No further rows: the reported perturbation-and-recovery result concerns stability of the subtractive solution, not neuron polysemanticity or a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No image classifiers or image-input neuron responses.
No transformer language models or token/context neuron responses.

Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by packing more sparse features than neurons. The handcrafted additive network illustrates packing by construction, which is not a result about trained networks.
No measurement of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or noise under sufficient capacity. Initialization is varied only to see whether the subtractive solution is recovered.
No comparison of polysemanticity shares across activations, architectures or regularization.
No examination of whether mixed neuron responses reflect one shared feature.
No comparison of measurement choices or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The rows and their ["none"] links are appropriate. The handcrafted networks are constructions, not trained results, and are correctly not recorded as rows. The perturbation-stability result concerns robustness of the solution and is correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test image classifiers or measure neurons responding to multiple unrelated image inputs.
Does not study transformer language models or neuron responses to tokens or contexts.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than neurons.
Does not measure polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise under sufficient capacity.
Does not compare polysemanticity rates across activations, architectures, or regularization, or report a performance-cost tradeoff for reducing it.
Does not examine whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a feature or are related jobs.
Does not compare ways of measuring neuron polysemanticity or explanation scores.

relation.reason: It takes superposition as background (the V3 mechanism) and studies computation strategies. It does not measure or test polysemantic neurons.

tranche.reason: Handcrafted and trained toy networks on an 8-pair name-memorization task, studying computation in superposition. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, and never tests any version (V1-V7). The handcrafted neurons covering four athletes each are a construction, not a measured result.

source_check.notes: Post on computation in superposition (8-pair name task, 6- and 2-neuron nets). It reports no polysemanticity rates, so it is not evidence on V1-V7. The test_reason's 'does not vary capacity' is loose: it trains 6- and 2-neuron nets, but measures no polysemanticity in either.
